# Fixture provenance

Only archives written by *other* implementations live here. Archives written by
bun-zipper are generated inside the tests instead: a fixture produced by the code
under test cannot judge that code, and freezing one would bless the next
regression that regenerates it.

Corrupt and hostile archives are also generated in-test, by patching bytes. A
blob named `crc-mismatch.zip` says nothing about *what* is wrong; the patch that
builds it does.

Each fixture below is paired with a test that first asserts the quirk is still
present. A newer tool version may stop emitting it, and a regression test that
quietly starts passing is worse than one that fails.

## Supplied by the project owner

Both store entries uncompressed (method 0), so a failure points at name handling
rather than the decompressor. Both hold `半角ｶﾅ.txt`, whose half-width katakana
are single bytes in CP932's 0xA1–0xDF range, and one entry in a subdirectory.

### japanese_filenames_utf8.zip

684 bytes, sha256 `8a1d91eba78e8acd07557ea11491d1880c4ba028ce52d32c9c777d4721d4a3fe`

Four entries with general purpose bit 11 set and UTF-8 name bytes — the
APPNOTE-standard encoding.

### japanese_filenames_cp932_legacy.zip

628 bytes, sha256 `fb0adeeb1ac5fa7a1da26905fbd9ec138b6d48c0a8d4125157fe933a326cff79`

The same four names in CP932 with bit 11 clear and **no** Unicode Path extra
field. Nothing in the archive records the encoding, so the caller must supply it;
this is the case that cannot be recovered automatically.

## Generated by `generate.ts`

Run `bun run test/fixtures/generate.ts` to rebuild these. They embed timestamps,
so the bytes differ on every run — the contract is the structural property below,
which `quirks.test.ts` asserts, not a checksum.

### 7zip_unicode_path.zip — 7-Zip 26.01, Windows

Non-ASCII entries carry local-codepage name bytes with bit 11 **clear** plus an
Info-ZIP Unicode Path extra field (`0x7075`) holding the real UTF-8 name. Reading
this correctly needs no encoding hint from the caller.

### infozip_short_central_size.zip — Info-ZIP zip 3.0, Windows

Written with `-UN=UTF8`, which combined with the NTFS security descriptor field
(`0x4453`) makes `zip` declare a central directory **shorter than the records it
actually wrote**. 7-Zip and Python both reject the result; Info-ZIP's own `unzip`
prints "reported length of central directory is too long ... Compensating".

The `-UN=UTF8` flag is load-bearing: without it the declared size comes out
consistent and the fixture tests nothing.

## Vendored from other projects — `vendor/`

| Directory | Upstream | License |
|---|---|---|
| `vendor/go/` | [golang/go](https://github.com/golang/go) `src/archive/zip/testdata` | BSD-3-Clause |
| `vendor/yauzl/` | [thejoshwolfe/yauzl](https://github.com/thejoshwolfe/yauzl) `test/success` | MIT |

Each directory carries the upstream `LICENSE` and a `NOTICE` naming its source.
Only `.zip` data files were copied; no Go or JavaScript source was taken.

These are conformance corpora curated over years of bug reports, kept because
**no tool on a developer machine can produce them**: macOS, WinRAR, and WinZip
output, archives with data prepended or appended, and hand-built adversarial
cases. `conformance.test.ts` names what each one exercises.

One is not a compatibility case but a security one: `comment-truncated.zip`
(Go issue 66869) hides a second end-of-central-directory record before a
deliberately truncated one, and must be **rejected**. A reader that skips the
truncated record and uses the hidden one extracts a different file than every
other tool reports.
